title: Literary Devices and Close Reading
tagline: How imagery, symbolism, irony, tone, figurative language and structure help shape meaning in drama, short stories and poetry for ISC Class XI Literature in English.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material and original practice questions written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI English Literature (Paper 2) syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). The prescribed works named here — Macbeth (Acts I and II), and the five short stories and five poems listed in the ISC Class XI prescribed texts — are identified because the ISC syllabus names them; the study material and all practice questions are original and are not taken from any CISCE examination paper. BoardPrep does not reproduce the set texts, so it does not replace reading them.

overview.intro: Literature questions in ISC Class XI are not just about what happens in a play, story or poem. They are also about how meaning is made: through imagery, tone, structure, figurative language and the choices the writer makes. This chapter gives you a way to talk about those choices. It is a reading skill chapter, not a plot summary chapter, and it is meant to work with the prescribed drama, prose and poetry of the Class XI syllabus.

facts.label: Prescribed works for Class XI
facts.value: Drama: Macbeth (Acts I and II). Prose: the five prescribed short stories from PRISM. Poetry: the five prescribed poems from RHAPSODY.

facts.label: Core ideas
facts.value: Close reading; imagery and figurative language; tone and voice; structure; dramatic methods; how form shapes meaning

learningOutcomes: Read a literary passage closely instead of only following the plot.
Identify and explain imagery, figurative language and sound effects.
Discuss tone, voice and point of view.
Explain how structure and sequence affect meaning.
Discuss dramatic methods such as dialogue, stage direction and character contrast.
Support observations with brief, relevant reference to the text.
Distinguish between what a text says and what it suggests.

blocks.text: Close reading means paying attention to the small things that carry meaning: a word choice, a pause, a repeated image, a sudden shift in tone. In literature questions, close reading is what turns a general opinion into a supported answer. The aim is not to count literary devices, but to notice how the text works and what that work does to the reader's understanding.

items: Read slowly enough to notice detail.
Ask what a particular word or line is doing.
Notice changes in tone, pace or perspective.
Connect details to the overall effect.
Keep answers tied to the text.

items.text: If a poem describes a scene in unusually sharp, cold-sounding words, that choice may matter even if the poem never explains it. The wording is part of the meaning.
items.note: Close reading notices what the writer has chosen to include and how it is phrased.

blocks.text: Imagery is language that appeals to the senses or creates a vivid picture in the mind. Figurative language includes simile, metaphor, personification and related devices. These are not decorations: they often do real work, such as making an idea concrete, suggesting an attitude, or linking one thing to another. When you discuss imagery, say what picture or impression is made and why it matters.

items: Describe the image, not just label it.
Explain what the image suggests or emphasises.
Notice recurring images, which may develop a theme.
Distinguish a literal description from a figurative comparison.
Connect imagery to mood, character or theme where relevant.

items.text: A storm image may simply describe weather, or it may also suggest turmoil, danger or change. The same image can do several things at once.
items.note: The best discussions say what the figure does, not just what it is.

blocks.text: Tone is the attitude a text conveys toward its subject. Voice is the sense of who is speaking or narrating, and how. Tone and voice are important in drama, prose and poetry, but they show up differently in each genre. In drama, tone may be revealed through dialogue and stage direction. In stories, it may be revealed through the narrator's attitude. In poems, it is often revealed through sound, diction and the speaker's stance.

items: Identify the attitude behind the language.
Notice whether the tone is serious, ironic, angry, tender, detached, comic and so on.
Ask how tone affects the reader's response.
Distinguish the speaker from the author where needed.
Track changes in tone within a text.

items.text: A character who speaks too confidently in a tense situation may create irony: the words say one thing, but the situation suggests another.
items.note: Tone is often visible in the gap between what is said and what is implied.

blocks.text: Drama is written to be performed, so it uses methods that depend on action and speech rather than narration. Dialogue reveals character and conflict. Stage directions shape movement, mood and staging. Contrast between characters can sharpen a theme. A good answer about a play pays attention not only to what characters say, but to how they interact and what the dramatist leaves for action and silence.

items: Notice what dialogue reveals and what it conceals.
Consider the effect of stage directions and pacing.
Look for conflict, contrast and repetition.
Think about the play's moments of tension and turning points.
Remember that a play is shaped for performance.

items.text: In Macbeth, the early emphasis on ambition, prediction and the tension between fate and choice helps shape the events that follow in Acts I and II. A close answer would look at how the drama presents that tension, not only at what happens.
items.note: This is a reading method, not a plot summary.

blocks.text: Structure is the arrangement of a text: how it opens, develops and ends, and how parts relate to one another. In poetry, structure may appear in line, stanza, rhythm or repetition. In short stories, it may appear in the order of events, the arrival of a surprise, or the way the ending changes the reader's view. Structure matters because it controls what the reader learns when.

items: Notice how a text begins and how it ends.
Ask what each part contributes.
Observe repeated words, images or ideas.
Think about timing, order and suspense.
Explain how the shape of the text supports its meaning.

items.text: A short story that saves an important fact for the end may change the meaning of all the earlier details. The ending does not just finish the story; it reorganises it.
items.note: Structure is a meaning-making choice, not just an outline.

keyPoints: Literature questions test understanding of how meaning is made.
Close reading notices specific choices, not general impressions.
Imagery and figurative language do work, not just decoration.
Tone and voice shape how a reader responds.
Drama uses dialogue, action and contrast.
Structure controls what the reader learns and when.
Always support literary comments with brief, relevant reference to the text.
examFocus: A good literature answer is specific: it names what the text does and explains why it matters.
Plot summary alone is not analysis; the question usually asks what the text means or how it works.
For prescribed texts, know the works well enough to make a short, accurate reference where the question asks for one.

vocabulary.meaning: Careful attention to the details and choices in a text.
Language that creates a vivid sensory impression.
Language used in a non-literal way, such as simile or metaphor.
The attitude a text conveys toward its subject.
The ways a play creates meaning through speech, action, contrast and staging.
The arrangement of a text and the order in which its effects are built.

questions.prompt: A good answer to a literature question is usually:
options: A full summary of the plot
A general opinion with no support
A specific point supported by reference to the text
A list of every literary device in the work
questions.answer: A specific point supported by reference to the text
questions.explanation: Literature questions ask for analysis, which needs a point and some support from the text.
questions.commonMistake: Retelling the story without answering the question.

questions.prompt: When discussing imagery, the best approach is to:
options: Name the figure of speech and stop
Describe the image and say what it suggests
Invent a meaning not in the text
questions.answer: Describe the image and say what it suggests
questions.explanation: Imagery is worth discussing because of the impression or meaning it creates.
questions.commonMistake: Labelling a device without explaining its effect.

questions.prompt: What is meant by 'tone' in literature? Give one example of a tone a writer might use.
questions.answer: Tone is the attitude a text conveys toward its subject. A writer might use a tone that is serious, ironic, tender, angry, detached or comic.
questions.explanation: Tone is the feeling behind the language, not just the subject matter.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing tone with plot or with the name of a character.

questions.prompt: Why can a play be understood differently from a story or a poem when it comes to revealing character?
questions.answer: A play reveals character mainly through speech, action and interaction in performance, while a story can use narration and a poem can use a speaker's voice. Each genre has different tools for characterisation.
questions.explanation: Different genres create character in different ways.
questions.commonMistake: Treating all literary forms as if they worked the same way.

questions.prompt: Explain how a writer might use structure to change the reader's understanding of a story by the end.
questions.answer: A writer may place an important revelation, reversal or final detail near the end so that earlier parts are seen differently. This can create suspense, irony or a shift in sympathy. The ending can reorganise the reader's view of what came before.
questions.explanation: Structure can reshape meaning, not just finish the text.
questions.commonMistake: Saying a story's structure is only its beginning, middle and end.
